items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ... I think there are a number of players that -­ >> [INTERVIEWEE] Jackie Byard.

ctx.x: But I think heard aspects of where the music was being pushed and brought some of that into what he did. I think there are a number of players that -­

Jackie Byard. Who aren’t avant-garde in that -- when you start talking about Joseph Jarman and all of that. But I’m thinking about the avant-garde as coming out of the early ’60s, up to ’64, ’65. Part of it has to do with how they approached form, the level of interaction of group improvisation, pushing the instruments past what were the conventional ways to play them, and the sheer force and energy of the music, which some people perceived as almost violent.
